opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it surprised me too. My mental model was still anchored a few years back, when a capable humanoid felt like something only a big lab or a well-funded company could afford. Then you look at what's coming out of the Chinese supply chain now and the price points are dramatically lower. That says a lot about how mature the hardware ecosystem has become: motors, reducers, batteries, sensors. A lot of that was already battle-tested in EVs, drones, and consumer electronics, so the robotics people are standing on that manufacturing base.

But I'd be careful about what conclusion to draw. Cheap hardware doesn't mean the problem is solved. If anything, it shifts the bottleneck more clearly onto intelligence. The body is becoming a commodity faster than the brain. You can buy a robot that walks, does a backflip, and looks great in a demo, but getting it to fold laundry in a stranger's apartment, robustly, without someone babysitting it, is a very different thing. That's a generalization problem, and it's fundamentally a learning and data problem, not a cost problem.

From my side, coming more from the model and research world, I actually find this exciting. Lower cost means many more robots in the hands of many more researchers and companies, and that means more real-world data. Data has been one of the core constraints for embodied AI. We don't have an internet-scale corpus of physical interaction the way we do for text. So if the hardware gets cheap enough that you can deploy at scale, you might finally get the kind of data flywheel that made language models work.

So my view is that it's a very good sign for the field, but people shouldn't confuse "the robot is affordable" with "the robot is useful." The second part is where the real work is, and I think it's still quite early.

r001.rationale: The response says Chinese supply-chain output has dramatically lower price points and treats this as evidence of a mature hardware ecosystem.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it surprised me, and I think it says something about where the real bottleneck is.

When I first started paying attention to humanoids, I assumed the hardware would be the hard part for a long time. Motors, actuators, battery, the whole mechanical stack. I expected these things to cost like a car, maybe more. And then you see prices come down to the range of a nice laptop or a cheap car, and you realize the hardware is riding the same curve that everything else in manufacturing rides, especially with the Chinese supply chain pushing on it. Once there is volume, the cost just collapses.

But I think the interesting part is what that reveals. If the body is cheap, then the thing that is actually scarce is the brain. A cheap humanoid that cannot do anything useful is just an expensive toy. So the whole question moves to the software side, to the policy, to the model. Can it generalize? Can it learn from a few demonstrations? Can it recover when it drops something? That is still really unsolved, and it is much closer to the problems I care about in agents and reinforcement learning.

So in a way the price drop is good news for people like me. It means the barrier to doing research is lower. You do not need to be a giant lab with a robotics budget to have a few of these in the room. More people can collect data, more people can try ideas, and that is usually how a field speeds up. I also think it creates a kind of pressure, because once the hardware is commoditized, there is no excuse anymore. The thing everyone is waiting for is the intelligence, and that is on us.

r001.rationale: It links the falling hardware prices to manufacturing scale and says the Chinese supply chain is pushing costs down, communicating its strength as a driver of lower costs.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s surprising, but it also makes me more interested in where the real bottleneck is. You can imagine the hardware becoming quite affordable, and yet the robot still can’t reliably do the things you want it to do. So the question shifts from “Can we build a humanoid robot?” to “Can we give it enough intelligence to be useful?”

The sticker price is only part of that. If you want a robot to help around the house, it has to handle unfamiliar objects, recover from mistakes, and work without someone constantly supervising it. A cheap robot that needs your attention all the time isn’t necessarily cheap to use.

So I’d take this as an encouraging sign for the hardware side. But I’d still want to see what it can actually accomplish, how reliably it does that, and how much human intervention it needs. That’s what would really change my expectations.

r001.rationale: The response calls the lower cost encouraging for hardware, but does not connect it to China’s strength in hardware supply chains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s exciting. It makes me update my assumptions about where the bottleneck is. If the hardware gets cheap enough, then the harder question becomes: can we build the intelligence that makes it useful?

A robot can be relatively inexpensive and still be very expensive per useful task if it needs constant supervision. So I’d want to know more than the purchase price. How reliably can it do something, how much human intervention does it need, and how long can it operate?

But cheaper hardware is a big deal because it lets more people experiment. You can deploy more robots, collect more experience, and iterate on the software. That could accelerate progress, even if the gap between an impressive demo and a useful robot is still substantial.

r001.rationale: The response says lower hardware costs are exciting and may enable more experimentation, but it does not connect them to China’s strength in hardware supply chains.
